draft.title: Why it began in Britain
card: The Industrial Revolution was the shift from making goods by hand to making them by machine in factories. It began in Britain in the 1700s.
Resources
Britain had plenty of coal to fuel engines and iron to build machines, and both were close to where factories grew up.
Money and empire
Wealthy people had money to invest in new machines. The empire supplied raw materials, such as cotton, and buyers for finished goods.
Farming
New farming methods grew more food with fewer workers. People who no longer needed to work the land moved to towns to find jobs in factories.
draft.remember: Britain had the resources, the money, the empire and the spare workers to industrialise first.

a.q: How did new farming methods help the Industrial Revolution begin in Britain?
opts: Fewer workers were needed on farms, so people moved to towns
They gave factories cotton to turn into cloth
They provided coal to fuel the new steam engines
They gave merchants money to invest in machines
a.why: Farms that grew more food with fewer workers meant many people could leave the land and take jobs in towns. Cotton came from the empire and coal was mined, so those options describe other causes.
a.clue: Think about what happened to the workers farms no longer needed.

b.q: Priya says Britain's empire helped its factories because it gave them somewhere to sell cloth and a source of cotton. Which statement is correct?
opts: She is right, as it gave markets and raw materials
She is wrong, as it gave only raw materials
She is wrong, as it gave only markets for goods
She is wrong, as it gave workers and coal
b.why: The card says the empire supplied raw materials such as cotton and also buyers for finished goods, so Priya names both roles. Saying it gave only one of these leaves out half of its part, and coal was found in Britain itself.
b.clue: Look at what the empire gave before and after goods were made.

a.best: Fewer workers were needed on farms, so people moved to towns

b.best: She is right, as it gave markets and raw materials

problems.detail: The right option stands out. It is the longest, and it is the only one not built as 'They gave/provided...' and the only one with a cause-and-effect 'so', so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.

The card says the empire supplied cotton. That is partly true (India, the West Indies), but from the late 1700s most raw cotton for British mills came from the United States, grown by enslaved people, and the US was no longer part of the empire. The card could note that cotton also came from trade beyond the empire.
